finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the caller's token with loose `==`. An attacker who knows a victim's email can reset the victim's password without the token. If $token comes from a JSON body, `true == "anystring"` is true on every PHP version. On PHP 7 and earlier, `0 == "nonnumeric"` is also true. Numeric-looking tokens such as "0e123" == "0e456" also compare equal under type juggling. The function is the loose twin of the correct reset_password(), which uses hash_equals.
finding.source: Attacker-supplied $email and $token arguments (presumably from a request). Precondition: the victim has a pending row in `resets`, and the caller passes the token as a non-string type such as a JSON boolean or integer. Only the call site could confirm that; it is not in this directory.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (line 5), which sets an attacker-chosen password for the victim account.

trace.note: Loads the stored token for the attacker-chosen email.
`$row['token'] == $token` uses loose comparison, so type juggling bypasses the check.
Password is overwritten for the target email, giving account takeover.

finding.guards_checked: No type cast of $token to string. There is no hash_equals, no expiry check and no single-use deletion of the token. SQL values are quoted with $db->quote, so there is no SQL injection. The strict reset_password() is safe against this, but this function is reachable if used. No callers exist in the directory, so the entry point is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none (no string cast, hash_equals, expiry or single-use check in reset_password_loose; only $db->quote for SQL, which is not relevant to the comparison)
verdict.reason: The loose `==` at reset.php:4 is real and unguarded, and the update at reset.php:5 follows it. But reset_password_loose has no callers, so I can't tell whether $token can arrive as a non-string such as a JSON boolean. Without that, only the rare "0e..." numeric-string collision applies.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are neither expired nor invalidated after use, in both functions. A token that was used, leaked or intercepted stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed to reset the password again. The `resets` table is never cleaned up and no timestamp is checked.
finding.source: Attacker who obtains an old or leaked reset token for an email (from email, logs, or referrer). No time bound applies.

trace.note: SELECT token only, with no expiry or used column.
Token compared. A matching token is accepted any number of times.
Password updated. There is no DELETE of the resets row afterwards.

finding.guards_checked: Looked for a DELETE or UPDATE on resets, an expiry column, and attempt throttling. None exist in this file. Token generation is not in scope, so token entropy is unknown. This is a design flaw that depends on how tokens are issued and stored elsewhere.

verdict.reason: reset.php:13-15 selects only the token, compares it with hash_equals, and updates the password with no expiry check, no DELETE of the resets row afterwards, and no throttling; the same applies to the loose variant at reset.php:3-5. The attacker must hold a valid token, so this is a token-lifetime weakness (replay of a used or leaked token), not an anonymous bypass.
